answers.label: Q1(a)
answers.finalAnswer: Where the Wind Goes
answers.solution: A suitable title: **"Where the Wind Goes"** (or "The Wind and My Kite"), because the poet wonders where the wind comes from and where it goes.

answers.label: Q1(b)
answers.finalAnswer: The wind is very strong: if he let go of the string, it would carry his kite away for a day and a night.
answers.solution: The poet thinks the wind is very strong. If he stopped holding the string of his kite, the wind would carry the kite away with it for a whole day and a night.

answers.label: Q1(c)
answers.finalAnswer: No. He could find where the wind goes by following his kite, but where it comes from nobody can know.
answers.solution: No. The poet feels he could find out where the wind goes: wherever his kite landed, the wind would have been going there too. But where the wind comes from remains a mystery that nobody knows.

answers.label: Q1(d)
answers.finalAnswer: It is very fast; it flies as fast as it can and he could not keep up with it even if he ran.
answers.solution: The poet thinks the wind is very fast. It is "flying from somewhere, as fast as it can", and he could not keep up with it even if he ran.

answers.label: Q1(e)
answers.finalAnswer: (iii) The poet knows nothing about the wind.
answers.solution:
(iii) The poet knows nothing about the wind. The poem opens "No one can tell me, Nobody knows, Where the wind comes from, Where the wind goes", and it ends by saying that where the wind comes from, nobody knows.

(Option (iv) can also be argued, since the poet notes the wind's speed and imagines finding where it goes; the option is also printed with a stray ":-". So (iii) is taken as the intended answer.)

answers.label: Q1(f)
answers.finalAnswer: (iv) Personification
answers.solution: (iv) **Personification**. In "It's flying from somewhere", the wind is described as flying, an action of a living creature.

answers.label: Q1(g)
answers.finalAnswer: keep up with
answers.solution: **keep up with** ("I couldn't keep up with it, Not if I ran.")

answers.label: Q2(a)
answers.finalAnswer: We have lost our old warm social life but cannot build a new one on the European standard.
answers.solution: Our home-life has become joyless because we have lost the warm, informal social life we once had, but we do not have the means to build a new one on the European standard.

answers.label: Q2(b)
answers.finalAnswer: They are no longer filled with informal gatherings, conversation and laughter, so they look empty and deserted.
answers.solution: The rooms and verandahs were once merry with the hum of conversation and laughter of informal gatherings. Today people visit only on business or duty, so they look empty and deserted.

answers.label: Q2(c)
answers.finalAnswer: Today people meet only for business, politics or social duty; in the past they met informally for the pleasure of meeting, with merry talk and laughter.
answers.solution: People of the present generation call on each other only on business, for political purposes or as a social duty. In the past, people met informally simply for the pleasure of meeting one another, and their gatherings were full of lively gossip and laughter, open to rich and poor alike.

answers.label: Q2(d)
answers.finalAnswer: No longer making opportunities to bring people together simply out of love for our fellow men.
answers.solution: Social miserliness, according to the author, is our habit of no longer making opportunities to bring people together simply because we love our fellow men. We are stingy with our company and hospitality and meet only when there is some business.

answers.label: Q2(e)
answers.finalAnswer: We should bring back warm, informal social gatherings and meet people for the joy of it, making everyone feel at home.
answers.solution: The author's message is that we should bring back the warm, friendly social life of the past. We should meet people simply for the joy of meeting, and make everyone, rich or poor, feel at home. Otherwise our lives will remain joyless.

answers.solution:
(i) lively: **animated** ("animated and amusing gossip")
(ii) devise or plan: **contrive** ("We have ceased to contrive opportunities")

(ii) Boring: **amusing** ("animated and amusing gossip"; 'merry' is also acceptable)

answers.label: Q3
answers.solution:
(Three topics chosen: (a), (b) and (d).)

**(a) Our Cultural Heritage**

India's cultural heritage is one of the richest in the world. It is the treasure of art, music, dance, languages, festivals, monuments and values that our ancestors have passed down to us over thousands of years.

Our heritage can be seen everywhere. The Taj Mahal, the temples of Khajuraho and the caves of Ajanta tell stories of great artists. Classical dances like Bharatanatyam and Kathak, and the music of Tansen, still delight people. Festivals such as Diwali, Eid, Christmas and Baisakhi teach us to live together in harmony. Above all, values like respect for elders and hospitality make us Indian.

Today, in the rush of modern life, many of these treasures are being neglected. It is our duty to protect our monuments, learn our folk arts and be proud of our roots. A nation that forgets its heritage loses its identity.

**(b) Co-education**

Co-education means boys and girls studying together in the same school. Most schools in India follow this system today, though some people still prefer separate schools.

Co-education has many advantages. Boys and girls learn to respect each other from childhood. Healthy competition in class encourages both to work harder. They learn to work together in projects, sports and cultural activities, just as men and women work together in real life. It also removes shyness and many wrong ideas about each other. Moreover, it is cheaper to run one school than two.

Some people fear that co-education may distract students. However, with good teachers and proper discipline, this problem is easily handled.

I believe co-education prepares children for a society in which men and women are equal partners.

**(d) A Chain is Only as Strong as its Weakest Link**

However strong the other links may be, a chain breaks at its weakest one. In the same way, a team, a family or a nation is only as strong as its weakest member.

Think of a cricket team. If ten players play well but one drops easy catches, the team may lose the match. In an army, one careless soldier on guard can put the whole unit in danger. In a country, if the poor remain uneducated and unhealthy, the whole nation cannot progress.

The proverb teaches two lessons. First, each of us must do our part well, because others depend on us. Second, the strong must help the weak instead of mocking them. When we lift up the weakest link, the whole chain becomes stronger.

answers.label: Q4
answers.solution:
B-24, Pitampura
Delhi
5 December 2019

The Editor
The New Times
Delhi

Subject: Alarming rise in population

Sir,

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw attention to the alarming rise in our population, which is visibly slowing the nation's development.

India's population has crossed 130 crore and is still growing every year. Our roads, trains, hospitals and schools are overcrowded. There are not enough jobs for the young, so unemployment and poverty keep rising. Forests are cut down to build houses, and water is becoming scarce. Whatever progress the government makes is eaten up by the growing number of mouths to feed.

The government must spread awareness about small families, especially in villages, and educate girls, since education is the best way to control population. Citizens too must understand that a small family is a happy family.

Yours faithfully,
Rehan

answers.label: Q5
answers.solution:
**Title: Good Manners Reveal Character**

Small acts reveal a person's character, just as tiny holes let in daylight, for character is built through daily deeds done well and honestly. Our behaviour towards others is its clearest test. Courtesy to everyone, whatever their position, pleases them because it shows respect, and pleases us even more. Anyone, rich or poor, can teach himself to be polite and kind. Like light, quiet gentleness influences society far more powerfully and fruitfully than loud force.

(75 words)

answers.label: Q6
answers.solution:
**Plastic Pollution: A Real Threat**
by Gaurav, Class VII, Modern School, Dehradun

Plastic is cheap, light and strong, so we use it everywhere: in bags, bottles, toys and packets. But the same strength makes it a terrible enemy of the environment, because plastic does not rot. A bag thrown away today will remain on earth for hundreds of years.

Plastic waste blocks drains and causes floods in cities. Cows and dogs eat plastic bags along with food and die painful deaths. Millions of tonnes of plastic reach the oceans every year and kill fish, turtles and birds. When plastic is burnt, it releases poisonous gases that harm our lungs. Tiny pieces of plastic have even entered the food we eat and the water we drink.

We can fight this threat. We should carry cloth bags, use steel bottles, refuse straws and say no to single-use plastic. Waste should be separated so that plastic can be recycled.

Let us remember: if we do not give up plastic, our planet may give up on us.

answers.label: Q7
answers.solution:
**The Pride of Rampur**

The moment Hari stepped down from the train he was greeted at the platform by the people of his small town. They had gathered there with garlands and a band. The drums began to beat and children shouted, "Hari! Hari!"

Only a month ago, Hari had been an ordinary boy from Rampur who ran barefoot on the dusty road to school every morning. His father, a poor farmer, could not buy him running shoes. Yet his sports teacher, Mr Verma, noticed his speed and trained him every evening on the village ground.

At the national school athletics meet in Delhi, Hari ran the 1500 metres against boys from the best academies. On the last lap he was fourth. Remembering the long road to school, he pushed with all his strength and crossed the finish line first, breaking the meet record.

Now, as the garlands piled up around his neck, Hari saw his parents crying with joy and Mr Verma smiling proudly. Hari touched his teacher's feet. "This medal is yours, sir," he said. The whole town cheered.

(a) Do you have a friend that you can **confide in**?
(b) You have been depressed for weeks; it's time you **snapped out** of it. ('it's time' is followed by the past tense)

answers.label: Q13
answers.finalAnswer: Preposition; Noun; Adverb; Adjective; Preposition
answers.solution:
(a) it was **past** 9 PM: **preposition** (beyond a time)
(b) talk about his **past**: **noun** (the object of 'about')
(c) a year had gone **past**: **adverb** (tells how the year had gone)
(d) **past** experience: **adjective** (describes 'experience')
(e) walked right **past** his friend: **preposition** (followed by its object 'his friend')

As printed, no word is underlined in (b); 'past' is taken as the intended word, as in the other parts.

answers.label: Q14
answers.finalAnswer: (ii) Cheek by jowl; (ii) Spilled the beans; (ii) Much of muchness; (i) Took him to the cleaners; (i) Come a cropper
answers.solution:
(a) at daggers drawn (bitter enemies): opposite (ii) **cheek by jowl** (very close and friendly)
(b) swept under the carpet (hid): opposite (ii) **spilled the beans** (revealed)
(c) like apples and oranges (completely different): opposite (ii) **much of muchness** (very much alike)
(d) greased his palm (gave him money as a bribe): opposite (i) **took him to the cleaners** (took his money from him)
(e) came off with flying colours (succeeded): opposite (i) **come a cropper** (failed badly)

(In (e) the sentence prints "come off" for "came off".)

answers.label: Q15
answers.finalAnswer: leaves; are playing; swam; have said; will have completed
answers.solution:
(a) The Howrah Express **leaves** (at) 5 PM. (simple present for a timetable; the stem drops 'at')
(b) They **are playing** the guitar now. (present continuous with 'now')
(c) It has been six years since he **swam** like this. (simple past after 'since' for a point in time)
(d) If I say something once I **have said** it a hundred times. (based on the saying "If I've said it once, I've said it a hundred times"; with 'say' in the if-clause, "say" can also be argued)
(e) By the end of this month we **will have completed** the work. (future perfect with 'by')

Part (d) is awkward as printed, so its answer is a judgement call.
